You pass if the template deduces
from its arguments and is constrained by a concept or a

that the caller tests before reading. An unconstrained template is a partial pass: it works, and T.10 asks for the constraint. A lookup that returns -1, 0 or a default value for a missing name is a fail, and so is reading the optional without testing it.

This page is about choices you can nail down before the program ever runs. A function template, or a class template, is not itself a function: it is a recipe the compiler uses to write one function per type you call it with, working out that type from the call's own arguments, a step called deduction. Writing the function for one type is instantiation, and what comes out is a specialization.
is a wrapper that either holds a
or holds nothing, and makes the caller check which before reading it.
holds exactly one of a fixed, closed set of alternative types, and knows which one through a hidden index: the type-safe form of a tagged union.

The problem each one solves is a different way of hiding a decision that should stay visible. Without a template, the same function is rewritten once per type, or pushed to run time to pay for a virtual call it never needed. Without
, "there is no answer" is written as a sentinel such as -1, which nothing forces a caller to check and which is sometimes a real value in its own right. Without
, "it's one of a known handful of kinds" is a raw union or a base class, and the compiler can't warn you when a switch or an override list forgot one of them.

How each works is selection at compile time. A template's type is deduced and, ideally, constrained by a concept, so a type missing the operations the body needs is refused at the call, not somewhere inside it. An
sits a value next to a flag, with no separate allocation. A
's alternatives share one piece of storage, and
, called with lambdas combined into one overload set, dispatches to whichever matches the live alternative, and the compiler checks that every alternative has a match.
What each costs you: an unconstrained template reports its errors deep inside a stranger's code instead of at the call; reading an
without testing it first is undefined behaviour, the same trap as an unchecked index; and a
only fits types fixed when you write it, not a set that grows after the program starts.
You meet all three in the interview question itself: a
template a type without an ordering can't call, and a joint lookup returning a motor id as
, empty when the name isn't in the table.

A variant is closed. Its alternatives are listed in one place, and adding one means changing every visitor, which the compiler then finds for you. A class hierarchy is the reverse, as the next topic shows: adding a type is one new class, and adding an operation touches every class. Klaus Iglberger's book
builds its comparison on exactly this trade (Guidelines 15 and 17), and Josuttis's C++17 book compares the two in section 16.4.3.
